Eyeball

GeometryCirclesTriangles
Game: Each circle sends two straight lines to the other circle, cutting out a short segment; see how the two segments compare. There is nothing to win or lose.
How to play: Drag the four blue points to move the circles or change their sizes. Tick the boxes for the helper circles and the rectangle, or press Reset to start again.

Drag A, RA, B or RB, or focus a point and press the arrow keys (Shift for bigger steps).

Look for the math

Two circles look at each other like eyes. From each centre, two lines just brush past the other circle; those lines cut the circle they started from. The surprising part is that the two cuts are always the same length, whatever the sizes of the circles.

Two fans of tangents

A tangent is a line that touches a circle at exactly one point, without crossing it. From centre A there are two tangents to the circle around B; from centre B there are two tangents to the circle around A. The applet draws all four rays. Where the rays from A cross circle A they mark P and Q; where the rays from B cross circle B they mark R and S. If one circle reaches inside the other, that pair of rays does not exist and the picture leaves them out.

Right triangles measure the cuts

Write d = AB for the distance between the centres, rA and rB for the two radii. A tangent meets the radius at its touch point at a right angle, so the Pythagorean theorem makes a right triangle with hypotenuse d. The angle at A therefore has sin = rB/d. The half of chord PQ is rA·sin, so PQ = 2·rA·rB/d. The logic test measured both chords on 2,140 arrangements, including circles almost touching and circles far apart; the largest gap between the claim and the measured lengths was below 0.000001.

Why the two lengths match

The expression 2·rA·rB/d does not change when A and B swap names. Doing the same right-triangle calculation at B gives RS = 2·rA·rB/d too, so PQ = RS — the page's claim, confirmed. The chords are also perpendicular to AB and their midpoints lie on it, so PQSR is a rectangle when its sides are drawn. This is not the Squinting Eyes Theorem of applet Eyeball2: there the equal things are the radii of two little curved triangles, 2·rA·rB/(rA+rB+d), not chords.

The extra circles

Tick Draw extra circles and the picture adds the circle on diameter AB plus two more through pairs of touch points. Each touch point sees AB at a right angle, so it lies on that circle — a cyclic quadrilateral in disguise. The Java applet that this page ports was embedded in the same cut-the-knot page, preserved in the Wayback Machine's 2009 capture; the live page now shows a GeoGebra version of the same theorem. The second circle starts outside the original 600×400 canvas, so this board is wider to keep every handle reachable; the construction is unchanged.

Drag the two centres closer together (without letting the circles swallow each other): the formula says both chords should grow together.
